name: DIY Botox for nose slimming

card.summary: Self-injecting botulinum toxin around the nose, which some forum users attempt in order to slim the nose and lift the tip without paying a clinic.
card.note: Botulinum toxin is a prescription drug; dermatologists, regulators and state health departments warn about self-injection, including misplaced toxin, counterfeit products and spread beyond the target muscle.

quick.overview:
Some looksmaxxing forum members describe injecting botulinum toxin themselves in or near the nose, aiming to soften a wide or drooping tip and give a slimmer, slightly lifted profile. The idea borrows from clinic treatments in which a trained injector relaxes a muscle that pulls the tip downward.

No published trial has tested self-injection for nose shape. Clinicians and regulators who have commented on the broader do-it-yourself toxin trend describe risks such as unapproved or counterfeit product, wrong placement, drooping or asymmetry that lasts for months, and rarely spread of the toxin through the body.
quick.how: Forum accounts describe ordering a pre-mixed Korean toxin product online and following diagrams of nasal muscles, then posting before-and-after photos. Specific placement, quantity and sourcing details are not reproduced here. Results from clinic nose-tip treatments are described as temporary, typically wearing off over a few months.
quick.risks: Botulinum toxin products for sale online may be unapproved, counterfeit or mislabelled. Misplaced injections near the face can cause weakness or asymmetry lasting months, and excess toxin can spread, with severe cases involving breathing muscles. The FDA has warned websites selling unapproved toxin, and dermatologists quoted by news outlets call self-injection dangerous.

lead: DIY Botox for nose slimming is the practice of people injecting botulinum toxin type A into or near the nose without a clinician, in the hope of narrowing the nose or lifting a downward-pointing tip. It circulates in looksmaxxing forums as a cheap alternative to clinic treatment and as part of a broader social-media trend sometimes called backyard Botox [1][2].

The appeal is a non-surgical change to nose shape. In clinics, a trained injector may target the depressor septi nasi, a muscle that pulls the nasal tip down when smiling, to produce a modest, temporary lift; self-injectors in forum posts describe attempting a similar effect and sometimes some slimming at the nostril sides.

No clinical trial has examined self-injection for the nose. Warnings about the wider do-it-yourself toxin trend come from dermatologists, a nurse injector, the FDA and California public health officials, who describe counterfeit products, placement errors and spread of the toxin [1][2].

chain: Muscle activity reduced for a few months
Claimed slimmer nose and lifted tip
angle.text: Forum users who attempt it say they want a less drooping tip and a narrower look without surgery or clinic fees. Clinicians describe any effect from nose-area toxin as temporary.

paras: Botulinum toxin type A blocks nerve signalling to muscles, which is the basis of its use for wrinkles, gummy smiles, jaw slimming and nasal tip lift in clinics. It is a prescription drug in the United States [2]. In looksmaxxing forums, users have posted accounts of ordering a pre-reconstituted Korean liquid toxin and injecting the nose themselves, sometimes posting follow-up photos.

Self-injection of toxin has spread through TikTok and Instagram videos, where people say cost is the main motivation. NBC News reported that a 100-unit bottle of Innotox is advertised for roughly 60 to 100 US dollars on third-party sites, against about 10 to 14 dollars per unit for Botox in US clinics. The same report says many learned techniques from social media videos [1].

Medytox, the maker of Innotox, told NBC News it sells only to authorised providers and does not endorse consumer self-injection. TikTok and Meta said content promoting Innotox violated their guidelines and was removed [1].
No studies found. No published trial has assessed self-injected toxin for nose slimming; research on toxin in the nose area concerns injections by trained clinicians and is not summarised here.

Dermatologist Michelle Henry told NBC News that unregulated aesthetic products are scary and dangerous, and nurse injector Molly O'Rourke said injecting is deeper and harder than people expect. Dermatologist Evan Rieder noted that online facial muscle maps are not accurate for everyone [1].

Reported risks include counterfeit, contaminated or poorly stored product; weakness or paralysis of the wrong muscles lasting months; delayed onset of effects of up to about two weeks, which can delay recognising a problem; and, with excessive toxin, paralysis of breathing muscles that can be fatal [1].

Writing in Science-Based Medicine in January 2026, Scott Gavura reported that the FDA issued warning letters in late 2025 to 18 websites selling unapproved botulinum toxin, citing adverse events including botulism symptoms, and that the California Department of Public Health warned of hospitalisations linked to counterfeit and improperly administered products. He noted that placement a few millimetres off near the eyelids or face can cause drooping, asymmetry, speech difficulty or trouble swallowing [2].

On looksmax.org, threads in which members describe self-injecting the nose and promise updates with photos have drawn replies ranging from requests for results to hostile comments. The wiki does not reproduce injection locations, quantities or sourcing from these posts.

timeline.event: FDA issues warning letters to 18 websites selling unapproved botulinum toxin [2].

lore.intro: Posts on looksmax.org describe self-injection as a cost-saving route to a slimmer nose and lifted tip, usually presented with a promise to share results later.

claims.claim: Toxin in the nose can slim it and lift the tip without surgery
claims.believers: Forum posters say the muscle that pulls the tip downward can be relaxed, giving a slightly lifted tip and a slimmer look for some months.
claims.experts: No published study has tested self-injection; clinicians quoted in news coverage emphasise placement and dosing precision as reasons injections are done by trained providers [1][2].

claims.claim: Self-injecting is a safe way to save clinic fees
claims.believers: Self-injectors cite price, convenience and instructions from online videos [1].
claims.experts: Dermatologists, a nurse injector, the FDA and California health officials report counterfeit products, wrong-muscle weakness and rare serious spread of toxin [1][2].
